title: A rules-based reason the team has not used: corporate bonds are allowed only through funds, and no dated corporate fund reaches the 2038-2042 payments

title: V5's 'no dollar asset is safer' is open to a ratings challenge; market pricing, not ratings, is the evidence that holds
problem: IPS V5 says 'Relying on one issuer for the roots may look like a weakness, but we accept it, since no dollar asset is safer.' A credit specialist knows the US is no longer AAA: BlackRock itself labels IBTM '99.97% AA Rated', while the corporate iBonds hold some AAA bonds (0.26-1.43%). On ratings alone the claim fails. What supports it is the market: on 14 Oct the AAA corporate index still paid 0.40% over Treasuries, and AA 0.60%, so investors price Treasuries as safer than even AAA companies. The [AI] suggestion 8 would delete the sentence (already flagged by UNIQ-07/JUDGE-05); this finding is about the evidence if any version stays.

title: Other governments' bonds: rule conflict unresolved, currency risk is about $10-12k per payment over 10 years, and hedging removes the gain
problem: Spreading issuer risk across UK, German, French, Italian or Dutch government bonds is the other obvious 'diversify the issuer' question. (1) Rules: the public Trading page lists those countries' Treasury bonds, but COMPETITION.md records that the logged-in session rules and the 6 Oct email say US Treasuries; unresolved. (2) Currency: Laura owes US dollars and the team cannot hedge (derivatives banned). One standard deviation over 10 years is about +/-25% for EUR/USD and +/-31% for GBP/USD (about $10-12k on a $50k payment); the worst 10-year fall in GBP/USD since 1971 is -56%. (3) Yield: unhedged international Treasuries (IGOV) yield 3.91% vs IBTR 5.18%, so such a ladder would cost roughly $39.5k more (rough MODEL). USD-hedged funds yield about the same as US Treasuries (GGOV 5.25%, IAGG 5.04% vs IBTM 5.05%) and never mature; whether a hedged ETF is allowed is an interpretation (UNVERIFIED).

title: The $1.4k room and a single default are small; a downgrade wave is the credit risk that matters, and the room cannot absorb it
problem: $1,372 of room is 2.74% of one $50k rung or 0.27% of the ladder's face. One issuer defaulting inside a 350-435-bond corporate fund costs a rung roughly $300-600 (ASSUMPTION: 1-2% weight, 40% recovery), which the room covers. The risk a credit manager would stress is a recession year where many BBB bonds are cut to junk together (S&P: global investment-grade defaults peaked at 14 in 2008, per FIIG), possibly in 2030-2036 when the corporate rungs mature. A Treasury rung has no such tail. Mixing up the two scales (single default vs wave) would weaken the answer.
